policy_title: Improve Maternity Care and Healthcare Management

verdict.plain: The policy sets an explicit, named target to close the Black and Asian maternal mortality gap — a severe racial disparity documented for over 20 years — which is a concrete equal-treatment commitment for a protected minority. The main caveat is that setting a target is not the same as closing the gap, and delivery depends on workforce and system changes that will take time.
verdict.biggest_unknown: Whether the explicit target translates into measurable reduction in the racial mortality gap depends on whether workforce, training, and anti-bias interventions are actually funded and delivered at scale.

verdict.rationale:
The dominant O9 signal in this policy is the explicit, named target to close the Black and Asian maternal mortality gap. Black women face nearly three times the maternal death risk of White women; Asian women face roughly double the risk; and these disparities have persisted for at least 20 years. Setting a public, measurable target for a named protected minority's health equality outcome creates an accountability mechanism that goes beyond aspiration — it is a concrete equal-treatment commitment directly within O9's scope. This earns a genuine 'improves' signal, albeit minor in magnitude because a target alone does not guarantee delivery, and the workforce and systemic changes required will take years.

The Cass Review commitment uses a soft verb ('work to implement') and NHS England was already committed to implementation before this policy, so the marginal O9 contribution here is limited. The evidence records that the Review recommended moving away from puberty blockers toward comprehensive assessment, and that some groups criticised its methodology — but no provided evidence unit establishes that implementation constitutes a restriction of equal treatment for transgender young people as a protected group under O9's criteria. The methodological criticism in E38 does not translate into a demonstrated equal-treatment harm; asserting otherwise would be an inferential leap unsupported by the cited evidence. Absent a grounded counter-claim, the false-balance rule requires the verdict to lean with the positive evidence rather than manufacture symmetry.

Overall: the racial-equality target is the only well-evidenced O9 effect; it improves equal treatment for a documented at-risk minority. Magnitude is minor because the policy instrument is a target, not a delivered outcome. Confidence is moderate because the baseline disparity is robustly measured but delivery is uncertain.

verifier.notes: All claims check out. Stated-tier quotes are verbatim from the policy text. Measurable-tier claims (E9, E10, E12, E36, E37) are supported by academic/institutional sources and the quotes entail the claims without overstating. E36 uses 'deemed unclear' which the claim faithfully reproduces. E37 supports the marginal-contribution framing in the rationale. Tier integrity is clean — no projections misclassified as measurable. Magnitude (minor) and time_horizon (this-parliament) are appropriate given the instrument is a target, not a delivered outcome. The rationale correctly notes the Cass Review commitment is soft and that NHS England was already committed, limiting marginal O9 contribution. The rationale does not impute motive or use party-identity framing. The methodological criticism of the Cass Review (E38) is acknowledged but correctly not elevated into a counter-claim without grounded evidence of equal-treatment harm — this is not false balance, it is correct application of the lean-with-evidence rule. No lever leakage: the verdict scores the racial-equality target for its effect on equal treatment, not on health outcomes per se. One minor observation: england.nhs.uk sources are typed as 'media' rather than 'government', which slightly undersells their provenance, but this does not affect the verdict's integrity.

evidence.snippet: Labour will ensure trusts failing on maternity care are robustly supported, train thousands more midwives, and set an explicit target to close the Black and Asian maternal mortality gap. They will digitise the Red Book record of children’s health and enable vaccinations for babies and children during health visits. The party will implement professional standards and regulate NHS managers, establish a Royal College of Clinical Leadership, and work to implement Cass Review recommendations for young people with gender dysphoria.

The Care Quality Commission (CQC)'s National Review of Maternity Services in England 2022-2024 found that 47% of maternity services were rated as "requires improvement" for safety, with 18% rated as "inadequate" and none as "outstanding"

Several high-profile independent investigations into failings at individual NHS Trusts (e.g., Morecambe Bay, Shrewsbury and Telford, East Kent, and an ongoing review at Nottingham University Hospitals) highlight a systemic need for improvement

The likely real-world effect of this policy would be a targeted effort to improve safety standards, address staffing levels, and foster a more supportive, learning culture within maternity units, moving away from a "blame culture"
The Health Foundation has previously supported projects aimed at improving safety culture in maternity units through training, measurement, and peer support

Training Thousands More Midwives**
Labour plans to train "thousands more midwives" as part of the NHS Workforce Plan

The Royal College of Midwives (RCM) has noted that the midwifery workforce has not kept pace with increasing demands, which are exacerbated by a higher proportion of pregnancies with complex medical and social needs, and policies for more personalized care
In 2022, 63% of midwives reported feeling unwell due to stress in the preceding year, and nearly a third of neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) shifts were not sufficiently staffed
The charity Tommy's welcomed Labour's pledge as a positive step towards a fully funded workforce

*   In 2020-22, women from Black ethnic backgrounds were almost three times more likely to die during or up to six weeks after the end of pregnancy compared to White women (Relative Risk (RR) 2.87, 95% CI 1.86-4.28)
Women from Asian ethnic backgrounds faced an almost two-fold increased risk
Asian women also had a slightly increased risk
*   These disparities have been persistent for at least 20 years
The King's Fund also reports that in 2020–22, the maternal mortality rate was about three times higher in Black women and about 1.5 times higher in Asian women compared with White women
Women living in the most deprived areas also experience more than twice the maternal mortality rate of those in the least deprived areas
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) does not directly collect ethnicity data on death certificates for maternal mortality, deferring to MBRRACE-UK reports for this specific information

The policy's real-world effect would be a focused national effort to understand and mitigate the factors contributing to these disparities, such as addressing racial and cultural bias in healthcare, improving management of pre-existing conditions, and enhancing access to equitable care, as highlighted by the Women and Equalities Committee
Tommy's welcomes this pledge, calling for it to be underpinned by comprehensive research and improvement programs

Digitising the Red Book Record of Children’s Health**
Labour intends to digitize the Personal Child Health Record, commonly known as the "Red Book," moving it onto parents' NHS apps
The Red Book, a paper-based record used for 30 years, contains vital information on a child's growth, development, and vaccinations
The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) has strongly advocated for digital child health records, stating it would be an "absolute game changer for child health services"

The real-world effects are expected to include improved data collection and sharing between parents and healthcare professionals, automated notifications for missed vaccinations or check-ups, and easier appointment booking through the app
This could significantly boost vaccination rates, particularly evident during recent measles outbreaks where a lack of digital records hindered quick identification of unprotected children
Previous governments, including under Matt Hancock, also aimed to digitize the Red Book by 2023-2024, but full implementation has not yet occurred
This initiative specifically targets families who face barriers to accessing vaccinations, such as travel costs, language difficulties, or vaccine hesitancy
Health visitors are considered trusted professionals who can effectively deliver this service
A Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) consultation in July 2025 revealed that 92% of respondents supported a statutory regulatory system, primarily to improve accountability and trust

The government plans to introduce secondary legislation for a statutory barring system, focusing on senior NHS leaders (board-level directors and their direct reports) who are found guilty of serious misconduct
The Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC) has been identified as the body to oversee this barring function
NHS England is also developing a comprehensive leadership and management framework, which will include a code of practice, core leadership standards, and a development curriculum

Credible organizations like Patient Safety Learning welcome these proposals, believing they will enhance accountability, reduce the "recycling" of poor leaders, and foster a more open and honest culture within the NHS
Managers in Partnership (MiP) also agrees with a limited barring system, finding it more feasible than full-scale regulation
However, MiP notes that many questions about the full implementation and scope of manager regulation still need to be answered

Establish a Royal College of Clinical Leadership**
Labour proposes establishing a Royal College of Clinical Leadership to "champion the voice of clinicians"
The Department of Health and Social Care has also committed to establishing a college of executive and clinical leadership
Hilary Cass

The final report, published in April 2024, recommended a holistic approach to care, emphasizing comprehensive assessment of individual needs (including neurodevelopmental and mental health conditions) rather than rapid medical pathways like puberty blockers, for which the evidence base was deemed unclear

NHS England is committed to fully implementing these recommendations, which include establishing new regional services and focusing on a research program to build a stronger evidence base for interventions
While generally welcomed by UK medical organizations, some groups have expressed criticisms of the review's methodology and conclusions

The Royal College of General Practitioners (RCGP) has updated its position in response, advising GPs not to prescribe puberty blockers outside of clinical trials and to leave gender-affirming hormones to specialists
